name: Çılbır (Poached Eggs with Garlic Yogurt)
description: Silky poached eggs on cool garlicky yogurt, finished with sizzling paprika butter.
steps: Crush the garlic with a pinch of salt and stir it into the yogurt. Spread the yogurt on a shallow serving dish and leave it at room temperature.
Bring a wide pan of water to a gentle simmer over medium heat and add the apple cider vinegar.
Crack each egg into a small cup. Swirl the water gently and slide the eggs in a few at a time.
Poach for 3 minutes until the whites are set and the yolks are still runny, then lift out with a slotted spoon and drain on kitchen paper.
Melt the butter in a small pan over medium heat until it foams, then stir in the paprika and dried mint for 15 seconds.
Place the eggs on the yogurt, drizzle with the hot paprika butter and serve straight away with warm bread.
tips: Use the freshest eggs you can find, as they hold their shape best when poached.
photo: Poached eggs resting on a pool of white garlic yogurt in a shallow white dish, streaked with glossy red paprika butter and a sprinkle of dried mint. Torn bread sits alongside.

name: Sucuklu Yumurta (Beef Sucuk & Eggs)
description: Spicy slices of beef sucuk sizzled in a pan with soft-set eggs, the classic Turkish weekend breakfast.
steps: Slice the beef sucuk into thin rounds, about 3 mm thick.
Heat the butter in a large non-stick frying pan over medium heat and fry the sucuk for 2 to 3 minutes, turning once, until it releases its red oil and edges crisp.
Reduce the heat to medium-low and push the sucuk slices to the edges of the pan.
Crack the eggs into the pan, spacing them out, and cook for 3 to 4 minutes until the whites are set but the yolks are still soft.
Sprinkle with black pepper and chilli flakes and scatter over chopped parsley.
Bring the pan to the table and serve with bread for mopping up the spiced oil.
tips: Sucuk is already salty, so you will not need to salt the eggs.
photo: A black cast-iron pan of golden fried eggs with bright yolks nestled among overlapping red-brown sucuk rounds, flecked with parsley. Torn crusty bread beside it.

name: Lahmacun
description: Paper-thin rounds of dough spread with spiced minced lamb and tomato, baked until crisp at the edges and served with lemon and parsley.
steps: Mix the flour, yeast and 1 tsp salt in a bowl. Add the warm water and olive oil and knead for 8 minutes until smooth. Cover and rest for 40 minutes.
Finely chop or pulse the onion, red pepper, tomatoes, garlic and half the parsley. Squeeze out excess liquid in a sieve.
Mix the vegetables with the minced lamb, tomato paste, paprika, cumin, chilli flakes and 0.5 tsp salt into a loose paste.
Heat the oven to its highest setting (about 250C) with two baking trays inside.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and roll each into a very thin round about 20 cm across.
Spread a thin even layer of the meat mixture over each round, right to the edge.
Bake 2 or 3 at a time on the hot trays for 6 to 8 minutes until the edges are crisp and golden.
Top with the remaining chopped parsley, squeeze over lemon and roll up to eat.
tips: Spread the topping very thinly so the lahmacun cooks quickly and stays crisp.
photo: Thin round flatbreads topped with a red-orange spiced lamb layer and charred edges, stacked on a wooden board with fresh parsley and lemon wedges.

name: İmam Bayıldı (Stuffed Aubergine)
description: Aubergines slowly baked with a sweet filling of onions, tomatoes and garlic, served at room temperature as the Ottoman classic.
steps: Peel the aubergines in lengthwise stripes and soak in salted water for 15 minutes, then pat dry.
Heat 3 tbsp olive oil in a frying pan over medium heat and fry the aubergines for 8 minutes, turning, until lightly golden. Transfer to a baking dish.
In the same pan, soften the sliced onions in 3 tbsp olive oil over medium heat for 10 minutes.
Add the garlic, diced pepper and chopped tomatoes with the sugar, salt and pepper and cook for 8 minutes until thick. Stir in the parsley.
Heat the oven to 180C. Slit each aubergine lengthwise and open it out like a pocket, then stuff with the filling.
Mix the water, lemon juice and remaining oil, pour around the aubergines and cover with foil.
Bake for 35 minutes, uncovered for the last 10, until very soft. Cool to room temperature before serving.
tips: Serve it the next day, when the flavours have had time to deepen.
photo: Four glossy dark-purple aubergines split open and brimming with red tomato and onion filling in a white oval dish, scattered with fresh parsley.

name: Burek (Meat Pie)
description: Crisp, flaky filo spirals filled with spiced minced beef and onion, the Bosnian bakery favourite.
steps: Grate the onions and mix with the minced beef, garlic, salt and pepper until well combined.
Heat the oven to 200C and oil a large round baking tin.
Mix the oil with the warm water. Lay a filo sheet on the counter, brush it lightly with the mixture and spread a thin line of filling along one long edge.
Roll the sheet into a thin sausage shape, then coil it into the tin. Repeat with the remaining sheets, joining the coils end to end into a spiral.
Brush the top with the remaining oil mixture and bake for 40 minutes until deep golden and crisp.
Cover with a clean tea towel for 10 minutes to soften slightly, then cut into wedges and serve with yogurt.
tips: Work quickly and keep unused filo covered with a damp cloth so it does not dry out.
photo: A golden-brown coiled spiral pie cut into wedges showing flaky layers and meat filling, with a bowl of white yogurt on the side.

name: Dushbara (Dumpling Soup)
description: Tiny lamb-filled dumplings floating in a clear mint-scented broth, an Azerbaijani comfort dish.
steps: Put the lamb bones and 1.5 litres water in a pot, bring to the boil, skim, then simmer gently with 1 tsp salt for 40 minutes.
Meanwhile, knead the flour, egg, 100 ml water and a pinch of salt into a firm dough. Rest it, covered, for 30 minutes.
Grate the onion and mix with the minced lamb, pepper and 0.5 tsp salt for the filling.
Roll the dough very thin, cut into 3 cm squares and put a tiny piece of filling in the centre of each. Fold into a small triangle and pinch the corners together.
Strain the broth and return it to a gentle boil. Drop in the dumplings and cook for 8 to 10 minutes until they float and the filling is cooked.
Crush the garlic with the vinegar and stir it into the soup with the mint just before serving.
tips: Keep the dumplings tiny, about the size of a thumbnail, as is traditional.
photo: A deep white bowl of clear golden broth with small triangular dumplings, sprinkled with dried mint and a few drops of garlic vinegar.

name: Lanzhou-Style Beef Noodle Soup
description: A clear, aromatic beef broth with chewy noodles, tender beef, white radish, chilli oil and coriander.
steps: Cover the beef shin with cold water in a pot, bring to the boil for 5 minutes and drain, rinsing off the scum.
Return the beef to the pot with 2.5 litres fresh water, sliced ginger, star anise, cinnamon, black cardamom and peppercorns. Simmer very gently, partly covered, for 2 hours.
Add the soy sauce, salt and the radish cut into chunks and simmer for another 20 minutes.
Lift out the beef, let it rest 10 minutes and slice it thinly. Strain the broth and keep it hot.
Cook the noodles in a separate pot of boiling water according to packet time, usually 3 to 4 minutes, and drain.
Divide the noodles between bowls, add beef and radish and ladle over the hot broth.
Top with sliced spring onion, coriander and a spoonful of chilli oil.
tips: Cook noodles separately so the broth stays clear.
photo: A large bowl of clear amber broth with noodles, sliced beef and radish, topped with green spring onion, coriander and a swirl of red chilli oil.

name: Circassian Chicken (Çerkez Tavuğu)
description: Poached shredded chicken in a creamy walnut and garlic sauce, topped with paprika oil.
steps: Put the chicken, halved onion, bay leaves and 1 tsp salt in a pot with 1 litre of water. Bring to the boil, then simmer gently for 20 minutes until cooked through.
Lift out the chicken and let it cool, keeping the stock. Shred the meat into thin strips.
Soak the bread in about 150 ml warm stock for 2 minutes and squeeze it lightly.
Blitz the walnuts (saving a few for garnish), bread, garlic and pepper in a food processor, adding stock gradually, until a thick creamy sauce forms.
Stir half the sauce into the shredded chicken and spread it on a serving plate. Pour the remaining sauce over the top.
Heat the olive oil with paprika for 20 seconds and drizzle over, then scatter with the remaining chopped walnuts. Serve at room temperature.
tips: Use the stock to adjust the sauce thickness: it should be like thick cream.
photo: Shredded chicken covered in a pale cream walnut sauce on a white oval plate, with a red paprika oil drizzle and crushed walnut garnish.

name: Iskender Kebab
description: Thin slices of spiced beef on cubed pide, covered with tomato sauce, yogurt and sizzling butter.
steps: Mix the lamb mince with the grated onion, cumin, paprika, salt and pepper, then shape into 4 flat oval patties (kofte-style).
Slice the beef sirloin very thinly against the grain and season with salt and pepper.
Simmer the tomatoes and tomato paste with a pinch of salt in a small pan over medium heat for 12 minutes until thick.
Heat the oil in a large frying pan over high heat. Sear the beef in batches for 2 minutes per side and the patties for 4 minutes per side.
Cut the pide into small cubes and toast them in a dry pan for 2 minutes, then lay them in the base of 4 plates.
Top the bread with beef, add the tomato sauce, then spoon a generous amount of yogurt alongside.
Melt the butter until it foams and turns light brown, pour it sizzling over each plate and serve with grilled green chillies.
tips: Pour the butter at the table for the best sizzle.
photo: Layers of sliced beef over golden pide cubes, red tomato sauce, white yogurt and a pool of butter, with a charred green chilli on the side.

name: Karnıyarık (Aubergine Stuffed with Beef)
description: Split fried aubergines packed with a savoury beef, onion and tomato filling and baked in a light tomato sauce.
steps: Peel the aubergines in stripes, soak in salted water for 15 minutes and pat dry.
Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat and fry the aubergines for 8 minutes, turning, until golden and soft. Drain on kitchen paper and move to a baking dish.
Fry the chopped onions in 1 tbsp oil for 6 minutes, then add the beef and brown for 6 minutes, breaking it up.
Add the garlic, 2 chopped tomatoes, half the tomato paste, salt and pepper and cook for 8 minutes. Stir in the parsley.
Heat the oven to 190C. Cut a slit down each aubergine and press it open, then spoon in the filling.
Top each with a slice of the remaining tomato and a pepper. Stir the remaining paste into the hot water and pour into the dish.
Bake for 25 minutes until the aubergines are completely tender. Serve with rice.
tips: Fry the aubergines in batches so they brown rather than steam.
photo: Four split aubergines filled with browned beef mince, each topped with a tomato slice and a green pepper, in a baking dish with red sauce.

name: Kıymalı Pide (Minced Beef Pide)
description: Boat-shaped breads with pinched ends, filled with spiced minced beef and baked until golden.
steps: Mix the flour, yeast, 1.5 tsp salt, water and oil, knead for 8 minutes, cover and let rise for 45 minutes until doubled.
Finely chop the onion, tomatoes, green pepper and parsley. Mix with the beef, tomato paste, paprika, pepper and 0.5 tsp salt.
Heat the oven to 240C with a tray inside.
Divide the dough into 4 and roll each into a long oval about 30 cm long. Spread the filling along the middle, leaving a 3 cm border.
Fold the long edges in over the filling and pinch the ends into points to make a boat.
Brush the dough with beaten egg and slide onto the hot tray.
Bake for 12 to 15 minutes until golden, brush the edges with butter and rest for 3 minutes before cutting.
tips: A very hot oven gives the best blistered crust.
photo: Four long golden boat-shaped breads with a visible spiced beef filling, edges glossy with butter, on a wooden board with parsley.

name: Turkish Mantı
description: Tiny beef dumplings topped with garlic yogurt and sizzling paprika-mint butter.
steps: Knead the flour, egg, water and 1 tsp salt into a stiff dough. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.
Grate the onion and mix with the beef, parsley, pepper and 0.5 tsp salt.
Roll the dough very thin and cut into 3 cm squares.
Place a small pinch of filling on each square and pinch the four corners together to form little purses.
Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil and cook the mantı for 8 to 10 minutes until they float and are tender.
Mix the yogurt with crushed garlic and a pinch of salt.
Melt the butter over medium heat, add the paprika, tomato paste and mint and sizzle for 30 seconds.
Spoon the mantı into bowls, top with garlic yogurt and drizzle with the butter.
tips: Tiny mantı take time, so let the kids help with the pinching.
photo: A bowl of small dumplings topped with white garlic yogurt and a red paprika butter drizzle with dried mint on top.

name: Ćevapi with Lepinja
description: Small grilled minced-beef sausages served in soft lepinja bread with raw onion and kajmak or sour cream.
steps: Mix the beef, lamb, crushed garlic, salt, pepper, bicarbonate of soda and sparkling water. Knead by hand for 5 minutes until sticky and smooth.
Cover and chill in the fridge for at least 1 hour, or overnight if you can.
Wet your hands and shape the mixture into about 20 finger-sized sausages, roughly 6 cm long.
Heat a grill pan or barbecue to medium-high and cook the ćevapi for 10 to 12 minutes, turning often, until browned and cooked through.
Warm the lepinja on the grill for 1 minute each side.
Serve the ćevapi inside or alongside the bread with chopped raw onion, sour cream and a sprinkle of paprika.
tips: Kneading well gives the ćevapi their traditional springy texture.
photo: A plate of golden-brown grilled ćevapi lined up beside a puffy flatbread, with raw red onion and a white dollop of sour cream.

name: Tavë Kosi (Baked Lamb & Yogurt)
description: Tender lamb and rice baked under a golden, custardy yogurt topping.
steps: Heat the oven to 180C. Season the lamb with salt, pepper and oregano.
Melt the butter in a pan over medium-high heat and brown the lamb for 8 minutes, then add the sliced onion and cook for 4 minutes.
Transfer to a baking dish, add the rice and water, cover with foil and bake for 1 hour until the lamb is tender and the rice has soaked up the liquid.
Whisk the eggs, yogurt and flour with a pinch of salt until smooth.
Pour the yogurt mixture evenly over the lamb and rice.
Bake uncovered for 30 to 35 minutes until the topping is set and golden. Rest for 10 minutes before serving.
tips: Full-fat yogurt gives the creamiest, most stable topping.
photo: A rectangular baking dish with a puffed golden-brown custard top over lamb and rice, with a slice taken out showing the layers.

name: Uzbek Plov
description: Fragrant rice cooked with tender lamb, yellow carrots, cumin and a whole garlic bulb, the national dish of Uzbekistan.
steps: Rinse the rice in several changes of water until clear, then soak in warm salted water for 30 minutes.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot over high heat until hot. Brown the lamb for 8 minutes.
Add the sliced onions and cook for 6 minutes until deep golden.
Add the carrots cut into thick matchsticks and cook for 8 minutes, stirring, until softened.
Add the cumin, pepper, salt and boiling water and simmer on low for 30 minutes to make the base (zirvak).
Drain the rice and spread it evenly over the meat without stirring. Push the garlic bulb into the centre and scatter the barberries on top.
Add hot water to cover the rice by 1 cm, cook on high until the water is absorbed, then poke a few holes, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 20 minutes.
Gently mix the plov from the bottom, then serve on a large plate topped with the lamb and garlic.
tips: Do not stir the rice while it cooks, or it will turn mushy.
photo: A mound of golden, glossy rice and carrots on a large platter, topped with chunks of lamb and a whole roasted garlic bulb.

name: Lagman (Hand-Pulled Noodles)
description: Chewy stretched noodles topped with a rich lamb and vegetable stir-fry sauce.
steps: Mix 450 g flour with 200 ml water and 1 tsp salt, knead for 10 minutes, rub with oil, cover and rest for 1 hour.
Heat 3 tbsp oil in a wok over high heat and sear the lamb for 4 minutes until browned.
Add the sliced onion, carrot and garlic and cook for 4 minutes.
Add the peppers and tomatoes, then tomato paste, cumin, pepper and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 5 minutes.
Pour in 400 ml water, cover and simmer for 25 minutes until the sauce is thick and the lamb tender.
Divide the dough into 8 pieces, roll into ropes, then stretch each rope and swing it to make long noodles about 1 m long.
Boil the noodles in salted water for 3 to 4 minutes until chewy and drain.
Serve the noodles in bowls topped generously with the sauce and chopped coriander.
tips: If you struggle with stretching, roll the dough and cut it into noodles instead.
photo: A shallow bowl of long pale noodles piled high with red-brown lamb and colourful peppers and carrots, garnished with green coriander.

name: Beshbarmak
description: Boiled lamb on wide hand-cut noodles with onions and a rich broth, the traditional Kazakh feast dish.
steps: Put the lamb in a large pot with 2.5 litres cold water, bring to the boil and skim off the foam.
Add 1 onion, bay leaves, peppercorns and 1 tsp salt and simmer gently for 2 to 2.5 hours until the meat falls from the bone.
Make the dough from the flour, eggs, warm water and 1 tsp salt, knead for 8 minutes and rest for 30 minutes.
Slice the remaining onions into rings and simmer them in a ladle of broth for 5 minutes.
Remove the lamb, strain the broth and cut the meat off the bone into pieces. Boil the peeled potatoes in some of the broth for 20 minutes.
Roll the dough thin, cut into 6 cm squares and boil in the strained broth for 6 to 8 minutes. Drain.
Serve the noodles topped with meat, potatoes and onions with dill, and drink the remaining broth from bowls on the side.
tips: The broth (sorpa) is served in a cup alongside the dish.
photo: A large platter of wide flat noodles topped with chunks of boiled lamb, soft onion rings and potatoes, sprinkled with dill.

name: Mercimek Köftesi (Lentil Patties)
description: Cold, spiced red lentil and bulgur balls served in lettuce leaves with lemon.
steps: Rinse the lentils and simmer in 500 ml water for 12 to 15 minutes until mushy, stirring often.
Stir in the bulgur, switch off the heat, cover and leave for 15 minutes to absorb.
Soften the finely chopped onion in the olive oil over medium heat for 6 minutes, then stir in tomato paste, cumin and paprika for 1 minute.
Mix the onion mixture into the lentils with chopped spring onions, parsley, salt and the lemon juice.
Knead with damp hands for 3 minutes until smooth, then shape into small oval patties.
Serve cold on lettuce leaves with extra lemon wedges.
tips: Wet your hands while shaping, as the mixture is sticky.
photo: Oval orange lentil patties arranged in fresh green lettuce leaves on a platter, with lemon wedges and parsley.

name: Baklava
description: Crisp layers of buttery filo with chopped pistachios, soaked in lemon syrup. Makes 24 pieces.
steps: Heat the oven to 170C and butter a 23 x 33 cm baking tin. Melt the remaining butter.
Make the syrup by boiling the sugar, water and lemon juice for 10 minutes until slightly thickened, then cool completely.
Chop the pistachios finely and mix with the cinnamon.
Layer 10 filo sheets in the tin, brushing each with melted butter. Spread half the nuts over the top.
Add 5 more buttered sheets, the rest of the nuts and finally another 10 buttered sheets, brushing the top well.
Cut into diamonds or squares with a sharp knife, going all the way through.
Bake for 45 to 50 minutes until deep golden, then pour the cool syrup evenly over the hot baklava.
Leave to soak for at least 4 hours before serving.
tips: Hot pastry and cool syrup keeps the layers crisp.
photo: A tray of golden diamond-shaped baklava with glistening syrup, each piece topped with bright green crushed pistachio.

name: Sütlaç (Baked Rice Pudding)
description: Creamy rice pudding baked until the top is caramelised in brown patches.
steps: Simmer the rice in the water for 12 minutes until soft and nearly all absorbed.
Add the milk and sugar and cook gently over medium-low heat for 15 minutes, stirring often.
Whisk the rice flour into the cold milk and stir it into the pot. Cook for 5 minutes until thick, then add the vanilla powder.
Pour into 6 ovenproof bowls and let them cool for 15 minutes.
Heat the grill to high and place the bowls underneath for 3 to 4 minutes until the tops are spotted dark brown.
Cool, then chill for at least 2 hours before serving.
tips: Watch closely under the grill, as the tops colour quickly.
photo: Individual terracotta bowls of creamy white rice pudding with dark caramelised spots on the surface.

name: Samsa (Baked Lamb Pastries)
description: Flaky triangular pastries filled with spiced lamb and onion, baked until golden.
steps: Mix the flour, 1 tsp salt and water into a dough, knead for 5 minutes and rest for 20 minutes.
Roll the dough into a rectangle, spread with half the soft butter, fold into thirds, then repeat the butter and folding once more. Chill for 30 minutes.
Mix the lamb with finely chopped onions, fat, cumin, pepper and 0.5 tsp salt.
Heat the oven to 200C. Roll the dough out thin and cut into 10 cm squares.
Place a spoonful of filling on each square, fold into a triangle and pinch the edges tightly.
Brush with beaten egg, sprinkle with sesame seeds and bake for 30 to 35 minutes until golden and puffed.
tips: Keep the pastry cold so the layers stay flaky.
photo: Golden triangular pastries dotted with sesame seeds, one broken open to reveal a juicy lamb filling, on a baking paper-lined tray.

name: Chak-Chak (Honey Dough Bites)
description: Crunchy fried dough strands bound with warm honey syrup and shaped into a golden mound.
steps: Whisk the eggs with 2 tbsp sugar and a pinch of salt, then add the flour and knead into a stiff, smooth dough. Rest it for 20 minutes.
Roll the dough into thin sheets and cut into strips about 5 cm long and 5 mm wide.
Heat the oil in a deep pan to medium-high (about 170C) and fry the strips in batches for 1 to 2 minutes until golden. Drain on kitchen paper.
Heat the honey and 100 g sugar in a large pan over low heat for 5 minutes until bubbling and slightly thickened.
Toss the fried strips in the syrup until coated.
Tip onto a plate, shape into a mound with wet hands and let it set for 1 hour. Break into pieces to serve.
tips: Keep your hands wet when shaping, as the syrup is very sticky.
photo: A glossy golden mound of honey-coated fried dough strands on a round white plate.
